column2: A four-wheeled robot you can talk to, driven from the touch screen or Telegram. It sees through a camera, plays music, follows objects in front of it, and stands guard. You build it step by step, from the battery up to the AI, with a small test at every step.
Status of this guide
Checked
All three full programs and the 13 test programs compiled successfully with Arduino ESP32 core 3.3.12 and the latest libraries.
Pins were chosen to avoid the boot, PSRAM and USB pins on both ESP32s.
The voltage of each module was matched against its datasheet.
Not checked yet
The complete robot has not been built and tested on real hardware yet.
The pin order of the TB6612 and the display differs between sellers. This guide was matched against photos of your modules, but still match the pin names printed on the board when you connect them.
The robot's voice uses an unofficial Google TTS service that can stop working at any time.
Three boards, one robot
Swipe the image sideways to see all of it.

The robot is split in three because one ESP32 does not have enough pins for everything. The Body (DevKit V1) handles what must be fast and safe: motors, sensors, stopping by itself. The Brain (ESP32-S3) handles the display, sound and internet. The Eyes (ESP32-CAM) only takes photos. The brain and body talk over 3 UART wires with simple text commands, so you can test the body on its own from the Serial Monitor.
Six parts, do them in order
Each part has small stages with a "it works" check. Tick the steps you finish; your progress is saved in your browser.
Battery, BMS, fuse, switch and three voltage converters. Measured with a multimeter before any board is connected.
Chassis, 4 motors through the TB6612, pan-tilt head, distance, tilt and weather sensors, STOP button, and the body code.
ESP32-S3 with a touch screen, SD card, speaker and microphone, then connected to the body over UART.
ESP32-CAM: upload through the MB board, view the photo in the browser, then move it to robot power and the pan-tilt head.
Telegram bot, Claude AI, speech to text, then the full brain code: face, chatting, seeing, follow and guard modes.
Final assembly
Layout on the three-level chassis, switching to battery power, testing on the floor, calibration, and a list of common problems.
Rules that apply in every part
Measure every voltage with the multimeter first. A converter that has not been set can output 8 V.
Battery switch OFF and USB unplugged every time you move a wire.
Add one module, test it, then continue. If it fails, you know the cause is in the last module.
Do all motor tests with the robot raised on a box, until Part 6.

Make sure the speed is 115200 baud, then press the EN/RST button on the board. Every test program prints a "=== TES ... ===" title at the start. On the ESP32-S3: if the upload log says USB mode: USB-Serial/JTAG, change Tools → USB CDC On Boot to Enabled.

Every stage ends with an "OK to lock in, or not yet" box. Lock in only what passed its test, does not need to be reached by other tests, and whose position is final. Bolts, cable ties and drilling into the plates wait for the dry stack in Part 6 Stage 1.
Boards and modules that send signals to each other must have their GND connected, even if their power comes from different sources. Check with the beep test.
Not sure about terms like voltage, GND, PWM, or how to use a multimeter? Read Basic Electronics for IoT and Microcontrollers first; the basics apply to this robot and other projects.

The ESP32-CAM needs no signal wires: only 5 V and GND. Its camera pins are already fixed on the board.
robot-ai-kode.zip: all the code in one file (3 full programs + 13 test programs, each in its own folder, ready to open in the Arduino IDE).
robot_badan.ino: for the DevKit V1 (board: ESP32 Dev Module).
robot_otak.ino: for the ESP32-S3 (board: ESP32S3 Dev Module, PSRAM OPI, Huge APP).
robot_mata.ino: for the ESP32-CAM (board: AI Thinker ESP32-CAM, Huge APP).
